answer_text:
The condition must be interpreted for distinct indices \(m\ne n\); otherwise no such sequence exists.

### 1. Necessary condition on \(a_2\)

Since adjacent terms must have gcd \(>1\),

\[
\gcd(a_1,a_2)>1,\qquad \gcd(a_2,a_3)>1.
\]

Choose a prime \(p\mid \gcd(a_1,a_2)\) and a prime \(q\mid \gcd(a_2,a_3)\). Both \(p\) and \(q\) divide \(a_2\).

If \(p=q\), then \(p\mid a_1,a_2,a_3\), so

\[
\gcd(a_1,a_3)\ge p>1,
\]

contradicting the condition because \(|1-3|=2\). Thus \(p\ne q\).

Therefore \(a_2\) must be divisible by at least two distinct primes.

### 2. Sufficiency

Conversely, suppose \(N\) has at least two distinct prime divisors. Pick distinct primes \(p,q\mid N\). Choose infinitely many new primes \(r_3,r_4,r_5,\dots\), none dividing \(N\), and define

\[
a_1=p,
\]
\[
a_2=N,
\]
\[
a_3=q r_3,
\]
\[
a_n=r_{n-1}r_n \quad (n\ge 4).
\]

Then every adjacent pair shares a prime:

\[
\gcd(a_1,a_2)=p>1,
\]
\[
\gcd(a_2,a_3)=q>1,
\]
\[
\gcd(a_n,a_{n+1})=r_n>1 \quad (n\ge 3).
\]

No prime divides two non-adjacent terms, since each new prime \(r_n\) appears only in \(a_n\) and \(a_{n+1}\), while the only other primes appear in adjacent positions or only in \(a_2\). Hence any integer with at least two distinct prime factors is possible as \(a_2\).

### 3. Four smallest possible values

The smallest positive integers with at least two distinct prime factors are

\[
6,\;10,\;12,\;14.
\]

Their sum is

\[
6+10+12+14=42.
\]

\[
\boxed{42}
\]
